yielded the following estimated ratios of olecranon process length to total ulna length for various
megaraptoran taxa and specimens:
Taxon Specimen Holotype? Ratio (approximate)
Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis FPDM 9712210 Yes 11.5%
Megaraptoridae indet. NMV P186076 N/A 12.7%
Megaraptoridae indet. LRF 100–106 N/A ? (not estimated due to incompleteness)
Australovenator wintonensis AODF 604 Yes 18.8%
Megaraptor namunhuaiquii MCF-PVPH 79 Yes 14.0%
Megaraptor namunhuaiquii MUCPv 341 No 15.3%
Joaquinraptor casali UNPSJB-PV 1112 Yes 20.3%
(The marked-up PDF version of our Suppl. Fig. 13 from which these ratios were estimated is
available upon request.)
As such, although, at an estimated 18.8%, the holotype of Australovenator comes close, at
20.3% the total length of the ulna, the olecranon process of Joaquinraptor is indeed
proportionally longer relative to the overall length of the bone than that of any other
megaraptoran. As such, we prefer to maintain “ulna with proximodistally enlarged olecranon
process” as a hypothesized autapomorphy of the new taxon. If the editors and/or reviewers
would mandate this, however, we could make this more specific by altering it to “ulna with
olecranon process that is 20% the proximodistal length of the bone.”
Is the enlarged olecranon process also present in Australovenator? But maybe it is due to a
different angle (the ulna shaft in the Australovenator is slightly anteriorly curved)? Please check.
Response: As explained in our previous response, the olecranon process of Joaquinraptor
(measuring from the proximodistal level of the anterior process of the ulna to the proximal end of
the olecranon process [and, therefore, the element as a whole]) is proportionally longer
relative to the remainder of the bone than that of Australovenator, Megaraptor, and every
other known megaraptoran (although, admittedly, it is only slightly longer than that of
Australovenator).
Other autapomorphies are quite clear.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment here, and naturally, we agree.
As a related aside, it is important to mention that the discovery of new fossils can sometimes
alter the status of what were previously considered autapomorphies of a given species or genus
into synapomorphies of a higher-level clade. This is particularly true for groups whose fossil
record is depauperate, as is presently the case for Megaraptora. As such, we acknowledge that
future discoveries may ‘transform’ some of the proposed autapomorphies of Joaquinraptor into
synapomorphies of Megaraptora or, more probably, clades within it.
5) The maxilla of the new megaraptorid is subtriangular, low, and elongated, somewhat similar
to, but also different from, the unenlagiine Austroraptor (from neighboring province, which also
stated in the introduction that unenlagiines are dominated in this area). So, a short paragraph on
the comparison/ differentiation of their maxillae might be good for clarifying that they are not the
same taxon/ clade.
Response: The general similarities of known skull elements of Joaquinraptor to those of the
large-bodied, penecontemporaneous unenlagiine maniraptoran Austroraptor cabazai are indeed
interesting, and are something that we hadn’t extensively considered before. As the reviewer
points out, both Joaquinraptor (and the juvenile specimen of Megaraptor MUCPv 595) share
with Austroraptor (and, probably, the large Brazilian unenlagiine Ypupiara lopai) a proportionally
low, elongate, and subtriangular maxilla that (we would add) houses low-crowned teeth. Though
this is, at this point, speculative given our incomplete understanding of the remainder of the
skeletons of these theropods, perhaps this hints at some degree of ecomorphological
convergence between the two forms, which might also explain why they seem to occur in
different areas of South America during the latest Cretaceous (large-bodied unenlagiines in
Brazil and northern Patagonia, megaraptorids in central and southern Patagonia). (In other
words, and although this is necessarily very tentative, perhaps large unenlagiines and
megaraptorids occupied similar ecological niches and/or exploited similar resources, but in
different geographic areas.)
That said, however, although the maxillae of Joaquinraptor and Austroraptor are similar in some
ways, they exhibit significant differences as well. For instance, the antorbital region is more
elongate in the unenlagiine, with the antorbital fossa being extremely attenuated, tapering
anteriorly to an acute point. Moreover, the maxilla of Austroraptor contains 24 teeth (Novas et
al., 2008b); the maxillary tooth count of Joaquinraptor cannot be definitively determined but it
was certainly substantially lower (approximately 15–17 based on the preserved morphology and
comparisons to the better-preserved right maxilla of MUCPv 595; Porfiri et al., 2014).
In sum, and following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added text to the relevant part of
our osteological description section to briefly compare the maxillae of Joaquinraptor and
Austroraptor (see tracked changes in the attached revision). If the editors and/or reviewers
would like, we could add further information, although given the already considerable length of
our manuscript it may not be advisable to significantly increase the amount of text here.
6) Focusing on the maxilla interdental plates of Joaquinraptor vs Megaraptor and the dentary
interdental plates of Joaquinraptor vs Australovenator vs Fukuiraptor. How are they different or
similar from each other? Please provide information. Is there any pattern or distribution of this
character in Megaraptora?
Response: Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added text (to the appropriate parts
of the description) comparing the maxillary interdental plates of Joaquinraptor to those of
Fukuiraptor kitadaniensis and Megaraptor and the dentary interdental plates of the new taxon to
those of Fukuiraptor and Australovenator. In short, at least as far as can be ascertained, the
interdental plates of Joaquinraptor and Megaraptor are unfused, whereas those of Fukuiraptor
and Australovenator seem to be fused. As such, and although this is unresolved at present,
unfused interdental plates could conceivably represent a synapomorphy of South American
megaraptorids or a subset thereof.
7) The scapula blade ratio: is it different from that of Megaraptor and Aerosteon and Aerosteon? Compared with
Gualicho (a probable carcharodontosaur closely related to Megaraptora or an elaphrosaurine)
which also exhibits fused scapulocoracoid, how are they different or related?
Response: We have searched the non-avian theropod literature, and unfortunately, we cannot
be absolutely sure what the reviewer is referring to by “scapula blade ratio.” Do they
potentially mean the anteroposterior (= craniocaudal or ‘proximodistal’) length of the scapular
blade divided by its minimum dorsoventral depth? If so, this is encapsulated by character 119 of
our phylogenetic analysis: “Scapula, blade length compared with minimum width of scapula
(Forster, 1999): less than 7.5 (0); more than 7.5 (1).” Joaquinraptor exhibits state 0, i.e., less
than 7.5, as do Megaraptor and Aerosteon. Gualicho shinyae, by contrast, exhibits state 1,
meaning that this enigmatic northern Patagonian theropod has a scapular blade that is
dorsoventrally narrower relative to its length than those of unquestioned megaraptorids. We
have added a sentence to this effect at the appropriate point of our osteological description.
8) Humerus deltopectoral crest: from supp. Fig. 5C, the deltopectoral crest looks somewhat
trapezoidal-shaped as in other megaraptorids (instead of subrectangular) (Supp. fig. 12) (please
check). But I agree that it is more robust in the new megaraptorid.
Response: As mentioned above, the primary objective of our Suppl. Figs. 8–16 is to compare
the overall appearance of various skeletal elements within Megaraptora (and in the case of
Suppl. Fig. 12, specifically the humerus). In our view, the deltopectoral crest of Joaquinraptor is
indeed subrectangular (as opposed to more trapezoidal) in shape, and that this morphology
may be readily observed in, among other figures, Suppl. Fig. 5C. As stated in our main text,
“Unlike in Australovenator, Fukuiraptor, and Megaraptor, the deltopectoral crest is
subrectangular in lateral view (Supplementary Fig. 5). Although, as in these taxa, the crest
projects prominently anteriorly and tapers proximally and distally, these features are less
marked in Joaquinraptor, with the exception of the juvenile Megaraptor (MUCPv 595) in which
the deltopectoral crest is small...” We therefore maintain “humerus with subrectangular
deltopectoral crest” as a proposed autapomorphy of Joaquinraptor, though we will attempt
to describe this same morphology in a different way (e.g., “anterodistal corner of humeral
deltopectoral crest pointed instead of rounded in lateral view”) if the reviewers and/or editors
deem this necessary.
9) Even though the new taxon clearly belongs to Megaraptoridae, some material could be
compared with other theropod clades, such as carcharodontosaurs, basal coelurosaurs,
tyrannosauroids, and some problematic such as Chilantaisaurus and Gualicho, for more
understanding of the evolution of Megaraptora.
Response: We agree that the Joaquinraptor fossils could (and potentially should) be compared
with the corresponding skeletal elements in selected non-megaraptoran theropods, such as
those mentioned by Reviewer 1, and indeed, we do already provide a few such comparisons.
That said, given the limited number of words that Nature Communications allows within the
main text, we chose to focus such comparisons on other indisputable and probable members of
Megaraptora, in order to provide a detailed assessment of the morphology of Joaquinraptor
relative to other representatives of this poorly known clade, and, in so doing and in that sense,
increase understanding of its evolution. As such, we would prefer to save extensive
comparisons of Joaquinraptor to non-megaraptoran theropods for a future, more
comprehensive osteology of the new megaraptorid.
10) Line 3939-396 “Patagonian megaraptorids present a suite of putative synapomorphies, such
as an elongated rostrum and a considerably enlarged manus, that suggest that these theropods
may have been evolutionarily and geographically differentiated from earlier diverging members
of the group (e.g., Australovenator).” – The elongated rostrum (at least dentary) and enlarged
manus are present in Australovenator (compare measurement of each element in
Australovenator and Joaquinraptor). So, this statement might be incorrect, or at least, must
include Australovenator.
Response: Although the reviewer is potentially correct in suggesting that the rostrum of
Australovenator may have been as proportionately elongated as is that of its South American
cousins (this is difficult to ascertain given that the only skull element yet known for
Australovenator is the dentary), the manus, or at least portions thereof, was undoubtedly
enlarged in Patagonian megaraptorids relative to, for example, the ulna (e.g., in the Megaraptor
holotype MCF-PVPH 79, the ulna measures 332 mm and manual ungual I measures 339 mm in
proximodistal length [Novas, 1998]; these same measurements are 267 and 187 mm,
respectively, in the Australovenator type specimen AODF 604 [White et al., 2012]). As such, we
maintain that South American megaraptorids exhibit synapomorphies that suggest that
these animals may have been phylogenetically and geographically differentiated from
their mostly more stratigraphically ancient Australian relatives. We have rephrased the
sentence as follows: “Although more evidence is needed, Patagonian megaraptorids present a
suite of putative synapomorphies, such as the absence of mesial denticles from the tooth
crowns, a manual ungual I that is subequal in length to the ulna, and a well-developed
‘mediolateral platform’ on the flexor tubercle of this ungual… that suggest that these theropods
may have been evolutionarily and geographically differentiated from earlier diverging members
of the group (e.g., Australovenator).” We will, however, simply delete the sentence if the editors
or reviewers mandate this.
11) Why Joaquinraptor is not the same taxon as Maip or Tratayenia? It was stated in the MS
that the coracoids and ribs of Joaquinraptor resemble those of Maip. If not much overlapped
material can be compared. Even though the phylogenetic analysis groups them into a single
clade, the different positions on the resulting tree(s) may be due to the artifact of, or biased by,
non-overlapped material. Please explain or state the reason or give evidence (apart from the
fact that they are from different provinces and rock strata) that they might be, or not be, the
same taxon.
Response: Here, we will begin by reiterating the fact that, as the reviewer pointed out,
Joaquinraptor, Maip macrothorax, and Tratayenia rosalesi all come from different
Argentinian provinces, regions of Patagonia, and rock formations (exposures of which are
many hundreds of kilometres apart from one another). They also come from different basins
and, most importantly, Tratayenia is certainly (much) geologically older than Joaquinraptor,
and Maip probably is as well. The geographic and stratigraphic provenance of each species is
summarized in the table below (data for Maip and Tratayenia drawn from Aranciaga Rolando et
al., 2022a and Porfiri et al., 2018, respectively).

(Patagonia) (Argentina) type locality distance from

Joaquinraptor Central Golfo San Chubut N/A Lago Maastrichtian N/A

As such, despite the fact that, with the exception of dorsal ribs (one complete rib and many
fragments of others in Joaquinraptor, two fragments in Tratayenia), there is no osteological
overlap among definitive specimens of Joaquinraptor and Tratayenia, it is a virtual certainty
that the two forms cannot represent the same taxon on the basis of geographic and
especially stratigraphic and temporal distance (i.e., at least 15 million years apart).
The stratigraphic and temporal correspondence of Joaquinraptor and Maip is much closer,
though also very probably not the same. Both these megaraptorids likely date to the
Maastrichtian, the final stage of the Cretaceous; within that stage, Joaquinraptor is at least
middle and more probably late Maastrichtian. The age of Maip is less clear, with most sources
(e.g., Aranciaga Rolando et al., 2022a) listing it as simply Maastrichtian without further
specification, which is unfortunate because the Maastrichtian is 6.1 million years in length
(72.1–66.0 Ma; see Walker and Geissman, 2022). Some recent publications (e.g., Novas et al.,
2019) even list the age of the Chorrillo Formation—the unit that yielded the Maip holotype—as
potentially extending into the late Campanian, i.e., late Campanian–early Maastrichtian. As
such, Maip is probably a few million years older than Joaquinraptor, although this cannot
presently be stated with absolute certainty (see also our response to Reviewer 2’s first point
below).
Fortunately, there is slightly more anatomical overlap between the holotypic specimens of
Joaquinraptor and Maip than there is between the former taxon and Tratayenia. Both
Joaquinraptor and Maip preserve dorsal ribs and the coracoid. As pointed out by Reviewer 2
(see below), the preserved dorsal ribs of Maip (identified as the first, second, and sixth; see
Aranciaga Rolando et al., 2022a) have features that are not present in the preserved dorsal ribs
of Joaquinraptor, namely multiple pneumatopores and a prominent, subtriangular medial flange
on the proximal half of dorsal rib 1 and seemingly more robust shafts in all preserved ribs.
Nevertheless, the absence of these features in Joaquinraptor could conceivably be due to
potential discrepancies in serial position of the dorsal ribs preserved.
With regard to the coracoids of Joaquinraptor and Maip, according to Aranciaga Rolando et al.
(2022a), the coracoid of the latter genus exhibits several diagnostic features, with hypothesized
autapomorphies indicated with an asterisk:
“… (4) prominent anterior projection on the coracoid*; (5) coracoid without a subglenoid ridge*;
(6) coracoid without a posteroventral fossa; and (7) and coracoid with ventromedial margin forming a
dorsoventrally deep articular surface for the sternum*.”
Unfortunately, the anterior margin of the coracoid of Joaquinraptor is broken away, so it is
impossible to determine whether characters (4) and (7) are present in the new taxon. That said,
characters (5) and (6) appear to be absent in Joaquinraptor (including a hypothesized
autapomorphy, character [5]), in that the coracoid of this taxon possesses a subglenoid ridge
and a posteroventral fossa. Please see the comparative image of the Joaquinraptor and Maip
coracoids in ventral or posterior (depending on how one orients this bone) view below:
Moreover, the posteroventral process of the Joaquinraptor coracoid is more strongly hooked
than that of Maip, as illustrated by the comparative image below:
In sum, based on the morphologies of the preserved bones, detailed anatomical comparisons to
other megaraptorans, and the results of our phylogenetic analysis, we consider Joaquinraptor
casali to be well supported as a new genus and species of megaraptorid. Despite the near-
total absence of overlapping bones, Joaquinraptor differs from Tratayenia in being very
substantially (i.e., at least 15 million years) geologically younger. The new taxon is also probably
stratigraphically younger than Maip, and moreover the coracoids and dorsal ribs of the two
forms exhibit multiple differences. We have added text to the diagnosis and descriptive
sections of our manuscript to highlight the morphological discrepancies between
Joaquinraptor and Maip.
12) Line 453-454 You stated that crocodyliforms could be one of the prey items for
megaraptorids. Could it be that these two animals just fight each other, like competition for food
while scavenging some carcass? Or, the other way around, the croc might come to eat that
‘dying’ megaraptorid, and they fought and got stuck in the mud. How or what concrete evidence
do you have to conclude this?
Response: In our view, the most likely explanation for this intriguing fossil association is
that the holotypic Joaquinraptor individual was in the process of feeding on (i.e., either
scavenging a carcass or eating a prey item it had killed) the crocodyliform when the theropod
perished. After all, the crocodyliform humerus was found between the near-articulated dentaries
of the megaraptorid, with some in situ tooth crowns of the theropod actually in contact with the
humeral shaft. However, following Reviewer 1’s comments, we have modified our text to
highlight other potential explanations for this association (see the Track Changes version of our
revised manuscript).
Additionally, it is important to note that a detailed taphonomic study of the Joaquinraptor quarry
and the fossils preserved within it is currently underway. Among other aspects, this study may
potentially support or refute whether the presence of this crocodyliform humerus at the site
constitutes evidence of dietary preferences in Megaraptoridae. (Interestingly, and perhaps not
coincidentally, Fiorelli [2010] described a peirosaurid crocodyliform with probable theropod bite
marks from the Bajo de la Carpa Formation of northwestern Patagonia. The largest known
theropod in the Bajo de la Carpa palaeoecosystem is the megaraptorid Tratayenia [Porfiri et al.,
2018].)
13) Fig. 4. and Line 397 onward – Why was Megaraptoridae absent in the north of Golfo San
Jorge Basin? Apart from the paleoenvironment, is there any evidence of island biogeography in
this area? For example, was Austral-Magallanes an island, that why megaraptorids were here
but not in the north of Golfo San Jorge Basin? If so, had the island influent to the
gigantism in Megaraptoridae?
Response: The reviewer raises an interesting point here; we had not sufficiently considered the
potential role that the latest Cretaceous palaeogeography of southern South America might
have played in the apparent provincialism of large-bodied theropods observed in central and
southern Patagonia (where megaraptorids appear to have been the apex carnivores) on one
hand and more northerly areas (in which abelisaurids and large unenlagiines seem to have filled
this niche) on the other. Interestingly, a recent palaeogeographic reconstruction of the region
during the Campanian (see Reguero and Goin, 2021:fig. 8) shows the depositional areas of the
Golfo San Jorge and Austral-Magallanes basins (i.e., central and southern Patagonia) as being
largely isolated from more northern areas by shallow seas and deltaic palaeoenvironments.
Alongside palaeoenvironmental and/or palaeoecological differences (see, e.g., the map of
proposed palynological bioprovinces in Vajda and Bercovici, 2014:fig. 3b), this could indeed
have been a potential catalyst for the differentiation of continental vertebrate faunas, including
non-avian theropods. We have accordingly added text to this effect at the appropriate
point in our manuscript and citations of Reguero and Goin (2021) and Vajda and Bercovici
(2014) to our bibliography.
14) Line 39 - a member of the derived megaraptoran[s] subclade Megaraptoridae. (add ‘s’)
Response: The phrase “derived megaraptoran subclade” is actually correct here (certainly more
correct than “derived megaraptorans subclade”) so we have not made this change.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Please see attached pdf
Response: We are grateful to Reviewer 2 for taking the time to review our manuscript, and for
their helpful comments.
I think that "Latest" should be replaced by "Late", because Maip comes also from lae
Maastrichtian beds from Chorrillo Formation....
Response: According to our review of the recent, relevant literature (e.g., Novas et al., 2019,
2024; Ghiglione et al., 2021; Aranciaga Rolando et al., 2022a; Moyano-Paz et al., 2022;
Perez Loinaze et al., 2023; Novas pers. comm. to MCL, 2024), the Chorrillo Formation of southern
Patagonia, Argentina—the geologic unit that yielded the exceptionally large-bodied
megaraptorid Maip macrothorax—is widely considered to be late Campanian–early
Maastrichtian, early Maastrichtian, or simply Maastrichtian in age (the latter without further
specification, which is unfortunate because the Maastrichtian is currently thought to be 6.1
million years in length [i.e., 72.1–66.0 Ma; Walker and Geissman, 2022]).
(For completeness’ sake, a paper published very recently, subsequent to our original
submission, by Perez Loinaze et al. [2025] states that “… palynological study of samples the
upper levels of [the Chorrillo Formation] supports an upper Maastrichtian age (not reaching the
K/Pg boundary)” and also “an upper Maastrichtian age for the Chorrillo Formation is proposed
supported by its palynological content.” As such, it is unclear whether Perez Loinaze et al.
[2025] are arguing that the entire Chorrillo Formation dates to the late Maastrichtian, or whether
only its uppermost levels are of this age. This is an important distinction to make because the
oldest/lowest Chorrillo horizons that Perez Loinaze et al. [2025] sampled are at roughly the 440
m level of the formation, whereas the stratum that yielded the Maip holotype is much lower in
section, ca. 170 m [see Perez Loinaze et al., 2025:fig. 2]. Consequently, Maip came from a
stratigraphic horizon that is 270 m below the oldest “upper Maastrichtian” level sampled by
Perez Loinaze et al. [2025]. How much time is represented by this 270 m span remains
unknown, but based on the conclusions of other recent authors [e.g., Ghiglione et al., 2021;
Moyano-Paz et al., 2022; Novas et al., 2024] we consider that the Chorrillo Formation
stratum that yielded Maip is most likely early Maastrichtian in age [or simply
“Maastrichtian,” if one prefers to be more conservative and less specific, as did Perez Loinaze
et al. [2023] in their earlier paper on the palynology and age of this unit].)
The age interpreted for the stratum from which Joaquinraptor casali was recovered is, at the
very least, middle Maastrichtian, and moreover, this horizon is probably situated near the top of
the Lago Colhué Huapi Formation, for which a late Maastrichtian age is well supported.
Therefore, Maip is probably a few (ca. 2–6) million years older than Joaquinraptor (see
also our response to Reviewer 1’s point 11 above). As such, we have chosen to retain
“Latest” within our manuscript’s title. However, we will gladly change this word to “Late” if
the editors and/or reviewers insist that we do so, as this revised title would remain accurate.
You should include here citations of previous works!
Response: Yes, we can certainly do so. We have added citations of older literature here, as
follows: Novas, 1998; Azuma and Currie, 2000; Calvo et al., 2004; Sereno et al., 2008; Hocknull
et al., 2009; and Porfiri et al., 2014. There are many other works that we could cite here, too, if
the editors and/or reviewers would mandate this.
These features are already present in other megaraptorids, particularly Megaraptor. I think
should be excluded from the diagnosis...
Response: This comment refers to the following features (numbered as in our diagnosis of
Joaquinraptor casali): ulna with (7) proximodistally enlarged olecranon process, (8) vertical ridge
on medial surface of proximal end, [and] (9) nearly straight shaft (but see below). Though we
appreciate Reviewer 2’s attention to detail here, we respectfully disagree with most of their
points. Again, the proximodistally enlarged olecranon process of the ulna is in fact unique to
Joaquinraptor, at least in terms of the degree to which it is developed proximal to the anterior
and lateral processes (see our response to Reviewer 1’s query 4.4 above). As for the vertical
ridge on the medial surface of the proximal end, to our knowledge this too is unique to
Joaquinraptor and not found in other megaraptoran ulnae (see Suppl. Fig. 6). Lastly, as we point
out, an ulna with a straight shaft is indeed found in Megaraptor namunhuaiquii, but only in the
holotype of this species, MCF-PVPH-79. The ulna of the referred specimen MUCPv 341 is
noticeably curved, which suggests that either MUCPv 341 is not referable to M. namunhuaiquii
or that this character varies between individuals of the same taxon. As such, we have elected
to retain characters (7)–(9) as proposed diagnostic features (specifically,
autapomorphies) of Joaquinraptor.
Here you should specify features that distinguish the new taxon from the coeval Maip. If you do
not find distinctive characters (in the case of Maip there are some bumps in the ribs, which are
absent in your taxon), you should make this explicit....
Response: As noted above (see our response to Reviewer 1’s point 11), it is difficult to
compare Joaquinraptor to Maip due to the incompleteness of known specimens of both taxa,
but especially the latter. That said, as Reviewer 2 points out, the dorsal ribs of the two taxa differ
in that the shaft of at least the first dorsal rib of Maip possesses a large flange or tubercle
whereas the ribs of Joaquinraptor do not. That said, however, this difference could be due to a
non-equivalence in the serial positions of the preserved ribs of these genera rather than
constituting legitimate evidence of their taxonomic distinction. More importantly, though, the
coracoids of Joaquinraptor and Maip differ in several respects, namely the presence of a hook-
like posteroventral process and a subglenoid ridge and posteroventral fossa in the former taxon
(see also above). Again, we have added text to better differentiate the two taxa in our
manuscript.
(Incidentally, and as also noted above, Maip and Joaquinraptor probably aren’t “coeval”; rather,
the former is most likely early Maastrichtian in age whereas the latter is probably late
Maastrichtian. Given that the Maastrichtian extended for 6.1 million years [72.1–66.0 Ma per
Walker and Geissman, 2022], the temporal distance between the two forms is likely very
considerable [ca. 2 Ma at minimum].)
[Delete “local”]
Response: We don’t see any issue with including the word “local” in this context, but we have
deleted it in accordance with Reviewer 2’s preference.
This bone is really different from that of other megaraptorids (and several theropods known to
me). Are you sure that is a postorbital? I think that if you are not certain, it can be safely
excluded from the description...
Response: We will concede that we have debated the identity of this bone ever since it was
discovered among the skeletal elements from the Valle Joaquín locality. Indeed, of all the bones
preserved in the quarry, this was perhaps the most difficult to identify, in part because it is
incompletely preserved but also because, whatever it is, it appears to be of somewhat peculiar
morphology. Accordingly, in our text, we make clear that our identification of this bone as a
postorbital is tentative (e.g., “The bone tentatively interpreted as the right postorbital...”). That
said, however, based on our comparisons of this bone to cranial elements of other megaraptorid
taxa, particularly Aerosteon riocoloradensis (Sereno et al., 2008; Aranciaga Rolando et al.,
2022b), Murusraptor barrosaensis (Coria and Currie, 2016), and Orkoraptor burkei (Novas et
al., 2008a), we have maintained the provisional identification of this bone as a postorbital.
I am not sure, but a work of Aranciaga Rolando et al. also discuss the pneumaticity in
megaraptorids (Aranciaga Rolando, M., Garcia Marsà, J., & Novas, F. (2020). Histology and
pneumaticity of Aoniraptor libertatem (Dinosauria, Theropoda), an enigmatic mid‐sized
megaraptoran from Patagonia. Journal of Anatomy, 237(4), 741-756.).
Response: Yes, the reviewer is correct, the cited paper by Aranciaga Rolando et al. (2020)
explores vertebral pneumaticity in the fragmentary and enigmatic Patagonian theropod
Aoniraptor libertatem (see also our Supplementary Information), which, contrary to what
Reviewer 2 states, is most frequently regarded as a non-megaraptorid megaraptoran as
opposed to a megaraptorid proper (see, e.g., Motta et al., 2016; Aranciaga Rolando et al.,
2020). Regardless, following the suggestion of Reviewer 3 below, we have deleted the
paragraph in question, rendering Reviewer 2’s comment here moot.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Dear authors,
I have reviewed the manuscript by Dr. Ibiricu and colleagues. The manuscript describes a partial
skeleton of a megaraptoran theropod dinosaur, which is substantially more complete than
known megaraptorans. Accordingly, the insights from the specimen provide new light on the
anatomy of megaraptoran dinosaurs, and the geological context of the fossil extends the
record of this clade into the latest Cretaceous.
The manuscript is high quality, the figures are excellent, and the writing is clear and succinct. I
have no major qualms with the research conclusions or methodologies. I feel that because of
the rarity and charisma of this clade, the manuscript will garner significant media attention.
Scientifically, this manuscript has a high likelihood of becoming well-cited, as its detailed
anatomical notes will be important for future work on these animals and their relatives.
Response: We appreciate Reviewer 3’s (Greg Funston’s) encouraging words here, and as with
the other two reviewers, we are grateful for the time he took to review our work, as well as his
helpful comments.
I have a few minor suggestions for improvement, which are generally optional and at minimum
involve only small changes to the text.
In the section on phylogenetics, it is argued that the position of Joaquinraptor in the tree
supports a tyrannosauroid affinity for megaraptorans (over an allosauroid one). This is presently
one of the major debates about these animals, and so I suspect this statement may draw some
flak because the specimen was included in a matrix which already found megaraptorans as
tyrannosauroid relatives. To me, the new analyses with this taxon do not necessarily improve
the support for the case, but they show that this new specimen is consistent with the hypothesis.
This is as we would expect: a late-branching form is unlikely to produce major changes in root
nodes, but this likewise means that its addition is not a very strong test of the former hypothesis.
If the authors choose, I feel that this potential weakness could be strengthened in one (or all) of
three ways:
either 1) a brief statement and revision to the wording explaining this debate in a little more
detail in the phylogenetic section, and explaining why this particular matrix was chosen when
others exist. It would be important here to mention that this phylogenetic approach is not
intended to test the position of megaraptorans within the tree, but of Joaquinraptor within
Megaraptora.
2) a broader discussion of the tyrannosauroid-like features of the anatomy of Joaquinraptor,
which might further strengthen the tyrannosauroid argument with characters outside of the
phylogenetic matrix (some of these characters might also be worth adding to the matrix, either
here or in future work);
or 3) adding Joaquinraptor to a matrix that finds megaraptorans as allosauroids, to test whether
its inclusion in that matrix changes patterns.
Response: As Dr. Funston surmised, the primary aim of our phylogenetic analysis was to
resolve the systematic position of Joaquinraptor within Megaraptora, as opposed to
evaluating the higher-level affinities of Megaraptora among Tetanurae. With that goal in mind,
we chose a phylogenetic data matrix that we felt was best suited to that purpose, namely the
matrix that includes (to our knowledge) the most comprehensive sample of megaraptoran
species and specimens of any published dataset. We have added language to clarify this
point; in other words, we have opted to follow his first recommendation above.
As a related aside, we agree that the higher-level phylogenetic affinities of Megaraptora
unquestionably merit further investigation, as do the interrelationships of the members of the
clade itself. With that in mind, some of us are currently involved in the description of new
Patagonian megaraptorid fossils that will also include a revised phylogenetic analysis of
megaraptoran affinities. Because that work (1) is being led by one of the present coauthors (as
opposed to the first author) and (2) entails a great deal of additional effort, we would prefer to
save it for a future publication.
My only other substantial comment regards the palaeohistological interpretations, and I feel that
these are a bit less optional. These are in two veins:
1) Age estimation should be done from the number of cyclical growth marks, which themselves
can comprise multiple LAGs. In this case, it appears that you have double and triple LAGs, and
the current interpretation of those features is that they together represent a single annual growth
mark (see Cullen et al. 2021 in Biology Letters). Anywhere that LAGs are paired closely
together, but this group is further away from other groups, they should be considered as being
formed in the same year and belonging to the same CGM. Revising these counts will not
change your overall interpretations of the maturity estimation, but they will put a younger age on
the specimen. In some ways, this might add more support to a coelurosaur identity, as
differences in growth patterns between tyrannosauroids and carcharodontosaurids are known
(see another Cullen paper: Cullen et al. 2020 in Proc B).
Response: The counting of growth marks and the establishment of minimum ages is always a
problematic issue, even more so in light of recent studies of extant taxa that show that the
number of Lines of Arrested Growth (LAGs) does not always represent the actual age of the
individual (e.g., Schucht et al., 2021). Therefore, the age estimation is necessarily tentative. In
accordance with what was stated by the reviewer, we have considered the multiple LAGs as
representative of a single growth cycle. For example, by enlarging our Suppl. Fig. 19D, the
reviewer will see that the arrowheads that indicate the position of LAGs 5, 7, and 9 (counting
from the perimedullary cortex to the outer cortex) are indeed double LAGs that have been
considered as a single growth cycle. These particular LAGs are very close together (around 40
microns or less) and resemble other double LAGs described in extant species. The reviewer
indicates that other groups of LAGs should also be considered as multiple LAGs, which would
reduce the estimated minimum age of the Joaquinraptor individual. Unfortunately, the criterion
proposed by Cullen et al. (2020) to determine whether or not they are multiple LAGs cannot be
applied here, since we do not have a complete section that allows us to determine whether the
groups actually originate from the split of a single line. Thus, since there is no criterion that
allows us to objectively determine whether the groups of LAGs indicated by the reviewer are
LAGs formed in different growth cycles (single LAGs) or LAGs formed in a single growth cycle
(i.e., multiple LAGs), we prefer to maintain the original age estimate.
2) I am not convinced that the preservation of the ICL in the rib is good enough to make many
comments on pneumosteon, and these, to me, are a weak part of the paper that doesn’t
contribute to the major conclusions. I would at the very least consider taking them out of the
main text, and if you wish to keep them, have them exclusively in the supplement.
Response: Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have deleted this part of the discussion
(and the citation of Lambertz et al., 2018) from the main text.
I am happy to be contacted by the authors, should they have any questions about my
suggestions.
Sincerely,
Greg Funston,
Visiting Assistant Professor
University of California, Davis
gfunston@ucdavis.edu
Response: We are grateful to Dr. Funston for his review and for making himself available to
answer any questions we may have.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Recent fossil discoveries have cast considerable light on the palaeobiology of Megaraptora, a group of large-clawed carnivorous theropod dinosaurs known from Cretaceous deposits in Asia, Australia, and especially South America. Nevertheless, many important aspects of megaraptoran morphology and evolution remain poorly understood, due in large part to the fragmentary nature of most fossils of these theropods and the scarcity of anatomically overlapping skeletal elements among the known taxa. Here we report a previously unknown megaraptoran genus and species represented by a partially articulated partial skeleton recovered from an uppermost Cretaceous stratum of the Lago Colhué Huapi Formation of south-central Chubut Province in central Patagonia, Argentina. Pertaining to the derived megaraptoran subclade Megaraptoridae, the taxon is among the most completely represented and latest-surviving megaraptorans. Its stratigraphic occurrence indicates that these dinosaurs likely persisted to the Cretaceous/Palaeogene boundary; moreover, the preservation of a crocodyliform humerus between the dentaries of the new theropod may provide information on megaraptoran dietary preferences and feeding strategies. Megaraptorids appear to have been the apex predators in central and southern Patagonian palaeoecosystems approaching the end of the Cretaceous, in contrast to more northerly areas of South America where these niches were occupied by other non-avian theropod groups.

---

## Introduction

Among the most mysterious of the many predominantly Gondwanan Cretaceous non-avian theropod dinosaur groups is Megaraptora, a tetanuran clade characterized by (at least in derived members of the group) elongate skulls with low-crowned teeth, extensively pneumatized bones, and, most strikingly, powerfully developed forelimbs equipped with hypertrophied unguals on the first and second digits 1–9. Although the stratigraphically oldest and earliest diverging representatives of this clade come from Asia 2,10–13 and Australia 14–19, megaraptorans are particularly abundant in South America, especially in the Late Cretaceous of Patagonia (e.g., refs. 1,3,4,6–8,20–32; see also Supplementary Notes 1 and 2). The evolutionary relationships of Megaraptora within Tetanurae—as either carcharodontosaurian allosauroids or early branching coelurosaurs, potentially basal tyrannosauroids—are controversial (see refs. 6,8,21,25,33–36, among others), due in large part to the preponderance of fragmentary, highly incomplete fossils of the clade and the scarcity of anatomically overlapping skeletal elements among the various megaraptoran taxa.

Here we report a new megaraptoran genus and species based on a well-preserved, partly articulated partial skeleton that includes cranial, postcranial axial, and appendicular elements, recovered from the Upper Cretaceous (Coniacian–Maastrichtian) Lago Colhué Huapi Formation of south-central Chubut Province, central Patagonia, Argentina (see Supplementary Note 3 for additional locality and stratigraphic data). Specifically, the new taxon, a member of the derived megaraptoran subclade Megaraptoridae, comes from a stratigraphic horizon only a few meters below of the top of this formation, establishing it as latest Cretaceous (Maastrichtian, probably late Maastrichtian) in age, and therefore one of the geologically youngest (if not the youngest) megaraptorans yet discovered. Moreover, because this taxon is also one of the most completely represented megaraptorans, it adds significantly to our understanding of the morphology, phylogenetic relationships, and palaeobiology of this enigmatic large-clawed theropod group. Furthermore, the unusually close association of a crocodyliform humerus with the type specimen of this theropod may provide information on the dietary preferences and feeding strategies of Megaraptoridae.

---

## Results

Systematic palaeontology
Saurischia Seeley, 1887 37
Theropoda Marsh, 1881 38
Tetanurae Gauthier, 1986 39
Megaraptora Benson, Carrano, and Brusatte, 2010 33
Megaraptoridae Novas, Agnolín, Ezcurra, Porfiri, and Canale, 2013 34
Joaquinraptor casali gen. et sp. nov.

Etymology. Joaquín, in tribute to the son of the first author (L.M.I.) and the informal name given to the locality when the skeleton of the taxon was discovered (Valle Joaquín); Latin, raptor, thief. Specific epithet casali in recognition of Dr. Gabriel Andrés Casal for his many contributions to knowledge of the Cretaceous palaeontology and geology of central Patagonia (including the formal recognition and naming of the formation from which this megaraptorid was recovered).

Holotype. UNPSJB-PV 1112, a partially articulated partial skeleton of a single individual that includes the mostly disarticulated partial skull (right maxilla, skull roof and braincase, probable right postorbital, right quadrate, both dentaries, in situ and isolated teeth), complete or nearly complete elements of the postcranial axial (atlantal intercentrum, three caudal vertebrae, dorsal ribs, other rib and probable gastralium fragments, haemal arch) and appendicular (left scapulocoracoid, humerus, radius, and ulna, right manual ungual II, left femur, much of the right tibia, the distal end of the probable right pedal phalanx III-3, the right pedal ungual III, and the possible partial left pedal phalanx IV-1) skeletons, and numerous indeterminate fragments.

Locality and horizon. Valle Joaquín, headwaters of the Río Chico, east of the southeastern shore of Lago Colhué Huapi, Chubut Province, central Patagonia, Argentina. Upper (Maastrichtian, probably upper Maastrichtian) stratum of the Upper Cretaceous Lago Colhué Huapi Formation (see below; also Fig. 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2).

Diagnosis. The holotype of Joaquinraptor casali is considered to represent a sexually but possibly not somatically mature individual based on the fusion of braincase sutures and the results of our osteohistological analysis, which reveal a reduction in the distance between growth marks in the outer bony cortex of limb bones (see below). Joaquinraptor is regarded as a member of Megaraptoridae based on its possession of the following suite of synapomorphies of the clade: (1) reduced anteriormost dentary alveolus 35; (2) absence of mesial denticles from tooth crowns 34,35,40,41; (3) olecranon process of ulna mediolaterally compressed, blade-like, and subtriangular in lateral view; and (4) ulnar shaft with well-developed, proximodistally oriented lateral crest or tuberosity 21,34–36. Joaquinraptor is diagnosed by the following autapomorphies (see also Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Figs. 3–7): (1) parietals strongly compressed transversely, narrower than frontals; (2) anterior margin of supratemporal fossa with sigmoid contour; (3) braincase lacking median septum in pneumatic recess (probably, but see below); (4) rugose atlantal intercentrum with well-marked lips and rectangular ventral contour; (5) middle or posterior caudal vertebral centra with well-marked elliptical lateral fossae that occupy more than half the lateral surfaces; (6) humerus with subrectangular deltopectoral crest; ulna with (7) proximodistally enlarged olecranon process, (8) vertical ridge on medial surface of proximal end, (9) nearly straight shaft (but see below), and (10) medially oriented, anteroposteriorly compressed distal end; and (11) distal end of radius crescent-shaped. Differs from the only other named Maastrichtian (probably early Maastrichtian and therefore stratigraphically older; see refs. 42–44) megaraptorid species Maip macrothorax in having a coracoid with a subglenoid ridge, posteroventral fossa, and hooked posteroventral process. The preserved dorsal ribs of Joaquinraptor and Maip also exhibit morphological differences, though these could potentially be due to non-equivalence in serial position rather than taxonomic distinction.
